passage:
Sahil,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it aloud, we both get tight in the throat.
I see you open the bank app every morning before you've even had tea. I see you study my face when my phone buzzes, as if you're reading a weather report. Last night you asked who "P" was in my messages. It was the plumber.
I understand why. After what I hid, your mind is trying to make sure you never get hit like that again. I don't blame you for it.
But I also see how tired you are. You aren't sleeping. And I feel like I'm living with an auditor, not a husband who is trying to forgive me. I don't know how long either of us can keep this up.
Could we find another way, together? I'll show you anything you ask. I'm your wife, not a suspect. I just want to be asked, not watched.
Dolma

qa.q: Who was 'P' in Dolma's messages?
qa.a: 'P' was the plumber.

qa.q: How does Dolma feel about being checked, and what shows it?
qa.a: Dolma feels hurt and suspected rather than forgiven; she writes that it is like living with an auditor, not a husband who is trying to forgive her.

qa.q: What could Sahil and Dolma try instead of the daily checking?
qa.a: They could agree on a planned, open time to look at money together, so Sahil gets reassurance without searching Dolma's face and phone every day. A counsellor could help them set it up.

qa.q: What is the checking costing Sahil himself?
qa.a: It is wearing Sahil out: Dolma notices he is tired and not sleeping, because his mind is on guard all the time against another shock.

grounding: Illustrates a husband's constant checking after a hidden loan, which wears him out and leaves his wife feeling watched instead of forgiven.

passage:
You asked how I'm doing, Hemant, so I'll be honest. Your old friend Raghav has turned into a bank inspector.
Every morning, before I've even brushed my teeth, I open the bank statement. Then I check it again at lunch. When Shobha, my wife, says she's going to her mother's, I watch her face while she says it, like I'm waiting for her eyes to slip.
Last week she laughed at something on her phone and my stomach dropped. It was a cat video. She turned the screen to show me without my asking, and her voice was so careful, so small.
I know why I'm doing it. After the loan, I promised myself I'd never be the last to know again. But I'm exhausted, yaar. I'm not catching anything. I'm just living in the second before the next shock.
And now she leaves her phone face-up on the table, all the time, like it's evidence.

qa.q: What was Shobha laughing at on her phone?
qa.a: Shobha was laughing at a cat video.

qa.q: Why does Raghav keep checking the bank statement?
qa.a: Raghav wants to make sure he is never the last to know again; after the loan, his mind is guarding against another shock.

qa.q: What turning point could Raghav look for at this stage?
qa.a: Raghav could tell Shobha how exhausting the checking is and ask for one full, open conversation about money, perhaps with a counsellor, instead of watching for clues alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Shobha to live with Raghav's watching?
qa.a: Shobha seems to feel watched rather than forgiven: her careful, small voice and the phone left face-up suggest she is trying to prove herself all the time.

grounding: Shows a husband's hypervigilance after a hidden loan: checking accounts and reading his wife's face, which exhausts him and makes her feel watched.

passage:
"Mohit, you've opened the bank app four times since dinner."

"Just checking the electricity bill went through."

"It went through yesterday. I showed you. I'm your wife, Mohit, not a case file."

"I know. I'm just... checking."

"You're checking me."

"Aditi, that's not fair."

"You looked at my face when my phone buzzed just now. I saw you."

"It was Sonal from your office. I read the name. Fine."

"You read the name?"

"I didn't mean to. My eyes just... go there now."

"Do you know what that's like? I wake up and you're already scrolling. I come home and you ask where I stopped for vegetables."

"I'm tired too, Aditi. I don't enjoy this. Every time I stop checking, my chest gets tight, like something else is going to fall on me."

"I told you everything. I said sorry."

"I know you did. I believe you. Mostly."

"Mostly."

"...I'm trying."

"So am I. It feels like being forgiven on probation."

qa.q: How many times has Mohit opened the bank app since dinner?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Mohit's tight chest when he stops checking suggest about why he keeps watching?
qa.a: It suggests he is anxious and on edge, trying to protect himself from another shock rather than wanting to catch Aditi out, and it is wearing him out.

qa.q: What could this couple try so that Mohit feels safe without Aditi feeling watched?
qa.a: They could agree on one set time each week to look at the accounts together, so Mohit gets his reassurance and Aditi is not checked at random moments.

qa.q: What is it like for Aditi to be watched after apologising?
qa.a: She feels watched instead of forgiven, "forgiven on probation", which leaves her hurt and tired even though she told him everything.

grounding: Mohit's constant checking of accounts and of Aditi's face shows hypervigilance after a hidden loan, exhausting him and leaving her feeling watched, not forgiven.

passage:
I noticed it first with the tea. Eshaan used to hand me my cup without looking up from his newspaper. Now he watches my face while I drink it, as if the answer to some question is written there.

This was a month after I told him about the loan I took for my brother. He said he forgave me. I think he meant it.

But he started checking the joint account every morning before brushing his teeth. When my phone rang, his eyes went to the screen before mine did. Once I laughed at a message from my cousin and he asked, too quickly, "Who's that?"

I am his wife, not a suspect. That's what I wanted to shout. But I also saw how grey he looked, how badly he was sleeping. He wasn't hunting me. He was bracing for the next blow.

Knowing that didn't stop it from hurting. I just felt watched in my own home.

— Harsha

qa.q: What does Eshaan check every morning before brushing his teeth?
qa.a: He checks the joint account.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel about being watched, and what softens it a little?
qa.a: Harsha feels hurt and watched, like a suspect at home, but also sees how grey and sleepless Eshaan looks, which brings some sympathy because he seems to be bracing for another blow.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Harsha at this stage?
qa.a: Harsha could name what is happening calmly, that the checking hurts and seems to exhaust Eshaan too, and suggest they find a way together to rebuild trust, perhaps with a counsellor.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be experiencing when he asks "Who's that?" too quickly?
qa.a: He is probably anxious and on guard, his mind trying to prevent another shock, and he may feel embarrassed afterwards at how suspicious he sounded.

grounding: Harsha describes her husband Eshaan's checking of accounts and her face after the hidden loan, and how it wears him out while leaving her feeling watched rather than forgiven.

passage:
Session note, 14 June

Uday and Kamini attended their third session. Uday arrived first and waited in the corridor checking his phone; when Kamini came in, his eyes went straight to her face and stayed there.

Uday described checking their accounts each night after she sleeps. He said, "If I stop, I feel I'm walking with my back to the door." He looked exhausted and mentioned losing sleep.

Kamini said she disclosed the loan to her brother in full two months ago and has hidden nothing since. "I am being punished for being honest," she said, and cried. Uday looked stricken at this.

I reflected back that his checking seems to be an attempt to prevent another shock, and that it is costing him rest and costing her the sense of being forgiven. Both agreed.

Next step: they will try a fixed weekly time to look at the accounts together, and we will review how it felt at the next session.

— Nilesh, counsellor

qa.q: What did Uday say it feels like if he stops checking?
qa.a: He said it feels like walking with his back to the door.

qa.q: What was Kamini feeling when she said she was being punished for being honest?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unfairly treated, as if her full disclosure had earned suspicion instead of forgiveness, and she cried.

qa.q: What does the counsellor's approach do well here?
qa.a: Nilesh names the checking as an attempt to prevent another shock rather than as an attack, so both can agree, and then offers a concrete next step, a weekly shared look at the accounts.

qa.q: Why might Uday look stricken when Kamini cries?
qa.a: He may suddenly see that his checking, meant to protect himself, is hurting her deeply, which likely leaves him guilty and torn.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows Uday's hypervigilant checking after his wife's hidden loan, how it exhausts him and makes Kamini feel watched rather than forgiven.

passage:
Sunday, late

I checked the bank app four times today. Jasleen doesn't know. Or maybe she does.

It's been six weeks since I found out about the loan. She's told me everything, I think. She cries when she talks about it. And still I look at her face when her phone buzzes, trying to read it. When she said she'd be late from the office on Thursday, I felt my stomach drop, and I asked three questions in a row like a policeman.

She said quietly, "Jatin, I feel like I'm living with a detective." She's right. I hate it too.

It isn't that I want to punish her. I think my mind is trying to make sure nothing surprises me like that again. But I'm so tired. I'm her husband, not her guard.

Maybe it's time to talk to someone about this. Both of us.

qa.q: How many times did Jatin check the bank app today?
qa.a: He checked it four times.

qa.q: What is Jatin feeling after six weeks of checking?
qa.a: He is exhausted and anxious, afraid of another shock, and unhappy about acting like a guard.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Jatin now?
qa.a: He could tell Jasleen honestly about the checking and suggest they see a counsellor together, as he is already considering.

qa.q: How does Jasleen experience Jatin's watchfulness?
qa.a: Jasleen feels watched rather than forgiven, as if living with a detective.

grounding: A husband keeps checking accounts and reading his wife's face after a hidden loan, which exhausts him and makes her feel watched.
